title: Why a pyramid structure
coreMove: Earn the answer through bottom-up grouping, then lead with it so the reader can judge support instead of assembling it.
sourcePressure: Chapter 1 explains why pyramid structure reduces reader burden: the higher point summarizes grouped support, groups must be logical, and communication runs top-down only after bottom-up thinking has earned the answer.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating the pyramid as a faster executive-summary style or a prettier outline instead of a discipline for deciding what the support adds up to.

sourceAnchors.name: nine-item grocery list
sourceAnchors.detail: the source sidecar says the explainer uses nine grocery items to show why grouped information is easier to hold and communicate than an unstructured list
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Nine groceries do not become easier because they are fewer; they become easier because the grouping gives the mind something to carry.

sourceAnchors.name: McKinsey interview notes
sourceAnchors.detail: the source sidecar ties Minto's origin support to frozen McKinsey interview notes and the three logical pyramid rules
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The consulting origin matters only because it exposed the same failure again and again: finished prose sitting on unfinished order.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective recognition, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm through a direct second-person passage, a short research/source aside, a reader question, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a nonprofit grant director turning scattered field reports into a board recommendation
exampleSpecs.audience: program leaders who write updates for trustees
exampleSpecs.stakes: a renewal vote depends on whether trustees can see the one funding decision inside twelve pages of field notes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sarah spreads twelve site reports across a folding table, sorts them into three labeled piles, and only then writes the one sentence the board should see first.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Fluorescent light falls across twelve stapled reports and three empty sticky notes.

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospital operations analyst summarizing weekend discharge delays
exampleSpecs.audience: clinical managers who distrust abstract dashboards
exampleSpecs.stakes: beds will stay blocked unless the delay sources become one usable operating claim
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Lukas moves each delay note under pharmacy, transport, or family consent, then deletes the headline he wanted because it no longer matches the groups.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A printer still warm from night shift spits out bed-delay notes.

exampleSpecs.domain: a city climate office preparing a council memo about flood sensors
exampleSpecs.audience: public servants converting technical material for elected officials
exampleSpecs.stakes: the council will postpone sensors if the memo reads like a research dump
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Camille compares the old chronology of findings with a revised answer-first structure that names the decision, then groups cost, risk, and maintenance beneath it.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Camille two drafts to notice the answer was hiding on page seven.

exampleSpecs.domain: a product support lead translating complaint tickets into a bug-priority note
exampleSpecs.stakes: engineers will chase anecdotes unless the tickets become grouped evidence
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Daniel asks which bug the tickets prove, predicts the wrong answer, then regroups the tickets by failure mode until the real priority emerges.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Which problem do 183 angry tickets actually prove?

exampleSpecs.domain: an archaeology lab manager writing a permit renewal report
exampleSpecs.audience: research staff who must justify field access
exampleSpecs.stakes: the permit can be delayed if artifact counts, site risks, and staffing constraints blur together
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Ingrid stop drafting, sort the permit notes into like kinds, and replace a broad top line with a narrower one the grouped evidence can support.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You are looking at trays of pottery tags and a half-written renewal letter.

exampleSpecs.domain: a logistics coordinator explaining port congestion to a retailer
exampleSpecs.audience: operations readers who need the destination before the detail
exampleSpecs.stakes: a costly rush-shipping decision will be made from the note
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Michael says the first draft is the port's diary, not the retailer's answer, then rebuilds it as one claim with three support groups.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "This is a diary, not an answer," Michael says beside the dispatch monitor.

skillTargets: tell answer-first communication from premature assertion
recognize when a top point truly summarizes support
use grouping to lower reader burden without deleting evidence
spot when bottom-up discovery has not yet earned top-down delivery

tryThisNowSpec: Take one live note stack and draw three boxes: loose facts, possible groups, earned top line. Do not write the top line until at least two groups have names.
